subfield: Quantum information science / atomic, molecular and optical physics
motivation: In 1995 Cirac and Zoller published the first concrete, physically realistic blueprint for a quantum computer. In it, trapped ions act as qubits and a shared motional mode acts as a quantum bus that mediates entangling gates. This idea turned quantum computation from an abstraction into an engineering programme, and the same bus concept later shaped other platforms, including circuit QED. Blatt's group realized the Cirac-Zoller gate experimentally. They went on to deterministic teleportation, multi-qubit entanglement of up to fourteen qubits, the first programmable quantum simulations, and early demonstrations of quantum error correction and logical-qubit operations. These measurements set new standards of fidelity and control. Together, this theory and experiment created a field: controlling engineered many-body quantum systems one quantum at a time. Their work underpins today's worldwide effort toward fault-tolerant quantum computers and quantum simulators.
